span-slicing.title: Slice an array with Span<T>
span-slicing.short: Reference a contiguous region without copying it.
span-slicing.summary: Span<T> lets you work with part of an array or buffer without allocating a new array.
span-slicing.why: A Span<T> is a view over existing memory, so writes through the span affect the original data.
span-slicing.tips: It is best for short-lived synchronous buffer work. Use Memory<T> when the data must cross asynchronous boundaries.

memory-buffer.title: Use Memory<T> across async work
memory-buffer.short: Pass a buffer region through await-based APIs.
memory-buffer.summary: Memory<T> is a memory view similar to Span<T>, but it can be stored and passed to asynchronous APIs.
memory-buffer.why: Memory<T> is not a ref struct, so it can survive across await boundaries.
memory-buffer.tips: Use .Span when you need synchronous element access.

ref-out-in-parameters.title: Choose between ref, out, and in
ref-out-in-parameters.short: Use reference parameters for different intent.
ref-out-in-parameters.summary: ref allows reading and writing an existing variable, out is for producing a value, and in passes a value by readonly reference.
ref-out-in-parameters.why: All three pass a storage location rather than a copy, but their initialization and write rules differ.
ref-out-in-parameters.tips: in is not automatically faster for small value types. Prefer clarity and measure performance.

yield-return-streaming.title: Stream values with yield return
yield-return-streaming.short: Return elements without building the whole collection first.
yield-return-streaming.summary: yield return lets the compiler generate the state machine needed for IEnumerable<T>.
yield-return-streaming.why: Execution resumes as enumeration advances, so values can be produced lazily on demand.
yield-return-streaming.tips: The iterator runs again for each enumeration. Be careful when the iterator has side effects.

async-enumerable-streaming.title: Consume IAsyncEnumerable<T> with await foreach
async-enumerable-streaming.short: Process asynchronously arriving values one at a time.
async-enumerable-streaming.summary: IAsyncEnumerable<T> lets consumers receive values as they are produced instead of waiting for the whole operation.
async-enumerable-streaming.why: await foreach advances the sequence by awaiting MoveNextAsync, which fits streaming workloads.
async-enumerable-streaming.tips: For cancellation, consider WithCancellation and EnumeratorCancellationAttribute.

semaphore-slim-limit.title: Limit concurrency with SemaphoreSlim
semaphore-slim-limit.short: Put an upper bound on simultaneous async work.
semaphore-slim-limit.summary: SemaphoreSlim can keep a large set of tasks from entering an expensive section all at once.
semaphore-slim-limit.why: WaitAsync acquires a permit and Release returns it for another waiter.
semaphore-slim-limit.tips: Call Release from finally so exceptions cannot leak permits.

datetimeoffset-conversion.title: Convert time with DateTimeOffset and TimeZoneInfo
datetimeoffset-conversion.short: Convert the same instant into another time zone.
datetimeoffset-conversion.summary: DateTimeOffset includes a UTC offset, making it useful for representing a specific instant without local-time ambiguity.
datetimeoffset-conversion.why: TimeZoneInfo.ConvertTime applies time-zone rules to compute the local representation of that same instant.
datetimeoffset-conversion.tips: Time-zone IDs can differ by platform, so verify the IDs available in the deployment environment.

httpclient-reuse.title: Reuse HttpClient
httpclient-reuse.short: Avoid constructing a new HttpClient for every request.
httpclient-reuse.summary: Long-running applications can reuse HttpClient and benefit from connection pooling.
httpclient-reuse.why: HttpClient is designed for multiple requests; constantly disposing clients can waste connection-management resources.
httpclient-reuse.tips: In DI-based apps, IHttpClientFactory is another option. Design timeout and cancellation behavior explicitly.

json-options-web.title: Use the web defaults for System.Text.Json
json-options-web.short: Start from common JSON settings used by web applications.
json-options-web.summary: JsonSerializerDefaults.Web applies a group of defaults commonly used by web APIs.
json-options-web.why: Its property-name behavior differs from the general defaults, which can better match client contracts.
json-options-web.tips: Configure shared JsonSerializerOptions once and reuse them when possible.

file-stream-async.title: Read a FileStream asynchronously
file-stream-async.short: Process a large file with a bounded buffer.
file-stream-async.summary: Repeated ReadAsync calls let you process a file without loading the whole file into memory.
file-stream-async.why: Each call returns the actual number of bytes read, so only that region of the buffer is valid.
file-stream-async.tips: The final read can be shorter than the buffer. Always use the returned count.

channel-producer-consumer.title: Connect producers and consumers with Channel<T>
channel-producer-consumer.short: Place an asynchronous queue between producers and consumers.
channel-producer-consumer.summary: Channel<T> from System.Threading.Channels safely passes data between asynchronous components.
channel-producer-consumer.why: A bounded channel can apply backpressure by making writers wait when consumers fall behind.
channel-producer-consumer.tips: Call Writer.Complete when production ends so readers can observe completion.

concurrent-dictionary-update.title: Update ConcurrentDictionary with AddOrUpdate
concurrent-dictionary-update.short: Express competing updates through the dictionary API.
concurrent-dictionary-update.summary: ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,TValue> supports thread-safe basic dictionary operations.
concurrent-dictionary-update.why: AddOrUpdate describes both the insert case and the update case in one operation.
concurrent-dictionary-update.tips: The update delegate can run more than once under contention, so keep it free of side effects.

periodic-timer-loop.title: Run periodic async work with PeriodicTimer
periodic-timer-loop.short: Express periodic work more clearly than a manual delay loop.
periodic-timer-loop.summary: PeriodicTimer represents a recurring asynchronous timer.
periodic-timer-loop.why: A loop around WaitForNextTickAsync handles both the next tick and cancellation as asynchronous waits.
periodic-timer-loop.tips: If the work can take longer than the interval, decide explicitly whether overlapping executions are acceptable.

task-whenall-results.title: Collect results with Task.WhenAll
task-whenall-results.short: Start independent async work together and await it as a group.
task-whenall-results.summary: Task.WhenAll returns an array of results after every Task<T> completes.
task-whenall-results.why: Creating the tasks first and awaiting them together avoids accidentally serializing independent operations.
task-whenall-results.tips: For very large workloads, combine this with a concurrency limit such as SemaphoreSlim.

cancellation-timeout.title: Compose cancellation and timeout tokens
cancellation-timeout.short: Combine caller cancellation with a time limit.
cancellation-timeout.summary: CreateLinkedTokenSource can stop work when either the caller cancels or a timeout expires.
cancellation-timeout.why: The linked token becomes canceled when any source token is canceled.
cancellation-timeout.tips: If timeout and user cancellation need different handling, also inspect the original tokens.

span-vs-memory.title: Span<T> versus Memory<T>
span-vs-memory.short: Prefer Span for short synchronous work and Memory when data must be retained or used asynchronously.
span-vs-memory.summary: Both represent contiguous memory, but Span<T> is a ref struct with strict lifetime rules.
span-vs-memory.why: Span<T> favors stack safety while Memory<T> can be stored on the heap and passed through async code.
span-vs-memory.tips: Keep API boundaries simple and choose the smallest abstraction that fits the lifetime you need.

ref-struct-lifetime.title: Understand ref struct lifetime rules
ref-struct-lifetime.short: Use stack-bound types without letting references outlive their data.
ref-struct-lifetime.summary: A ref struct can safely contain stack-bound data such as Span<T>.
ref-struct-lifetime.why: Compiler restrictions prevent the value from escaping to the heap and outliving the memory it references.
ref-struct-lifetime.tips: When data must cross class or async boundaries, consider an owning array or Memory<T> instead.

generic-constraints-design.title: Express requirements with generic constraints
generic-constraints-design.short: Describe what T must support with where clauses.
generic-constraints-design.summary: Generic constraints state compile-time requirements for type arguments.
generic-constraints-design.why: They enable more operations inside generic code and reject incompatible type arguments early.
generic-constraints-design.tips: Too many constraints reduce reuse, so require only what the implementation actually needs.

required-members.title: Require initialization with required members
required-members.short: Force callers to initialize designated members when creating an object.
required-members.summary: The required modifier tells the compiler that selected members must be initialized during object creation.
required-members.why: It expresses a construction-time contract that nullable annotations alone do not fully capture.
required-members.tips: When combining required members with constructors, understand the role of SetsRequiredMembersAttribute.

collection-expressions.title: Use collection expressions [...]
collection-expressions.short: Initialize arrays, lists, and other collection targets with one concise syntax.
collection-expressions.summary: C# collection expressions can initialize several collection types with a common syntax.
collection-expressions.why: The target type influences how the expression is materialized, so the right-hand side alone may not determine the final type.
collection-expressions.tips: Prefer readability and make the target type explicit when inference would be unclear.

valuetask-guidance.title: Know when ValueTask is appropriate
valuetask-guidance.short: It is not a universally cheaper Task.
valuetask-guidance.summary: ValueTask<T> can avoid Task<T> allocation on hot paths that complete synchronously very often.
valuetask-guidance.why: Because it is a struct with more usage rules, Task<T> is simpler for most asynchronous APIs.
valuetask-guidance.tips: Use it when measurement shows allocation pressure that ValueTask can meaningfully reduce.

cancellation-cooperation.title: Cancellation is cooperative
cancellation-cooperation.short: Receiving a CancellationToken does not stop work by itself.
cancellation-cooperation.summary: CancellationToken is a cooperative signal rather than a forced thread-abort mechanism.
cancellation-cooperation.why: Cancellation propagates when code passes the token to lower-level APIs or checks ThrowIfCancellationRequested.
cancellation-cooperation.tips: Long CPU loops should also check the token at sensible intervals.

synchronization-context.title: Understand SynchronizationContext and await continuation
synchronization-context.short: Know where code may resume after await in UI-style applications.
synchronization-context.summary: Some environments capture the current SynchronizationContext so an await continuation resumes on that context.
synchronization-context.why: This is useful for UI-thread affinity, but synchronous blocking can turn the same behavior into a deadlock risk.
synchronization-context.tips: Library code and UI code often have different context requirements.

exception-filters.title: Use exception filters with when
exception-filters.short: Narrow a catch clause without catching and rethrowing manually.
exception-filters.summary: catch (...) when (...) handles an exception only when both the type and the filter condition match.
exception-filters.why: If the filter is false, that catch clause is skipped and normal exception propagation continues.
exception-filters.tips: Keep filter expressions free of state-changing side effects for easier debugging.

datetime-kind-model.title: Understand the three DateTime.Kind states
datetime-kind-model.short: Do not confuse Utc, Local, and Unspecified.
datetime-kind-model.summary: DateTime.Kind indicates whether a value should be interpreted as UTC, local time, or time-zone unspecified.
datetime-kind-model.why: The same displayed clock value can be interpreted differently by conversion APIs depending on Kind.
datetime-kind-model.tips: For system boundaries, prefer DateTimeOffset or UTC when possible to reduce ambiguity.

equality-comparer-design.title: Treat EqualityComparer as part of collection design
equality-comparer-design.short: Choose key identity rules when creating the collection.
equality-comparer-design.summary: Dictionary and HashSet can use IEqualityComparer<T> to change equality and hash-code behavior.
equality-comparer-design.why: This lets domain identity rules such as case-insensitive string keys be expressed directly by the collection.
equality-comparer-design.tips: Make the comparer explicit at construction instead of trying to change identity rules later.

variance-generic-interfaces.title: Understand covariance and contravariance
variance-generic-interfaces.short: out and in type parameters affect assignment compatibility.
variance-generic-interfaces.summary: Covariance allows some conversions from a more specific type to a base type, while contravariance supports the opposite direction for certain interfaces and delegates.
variance-generic-interfaces.why: The compiler permits these conversions when the type parameter is used safely only as output or only as input.
variance-generic-interfaces.tips: Mutable types such as List<T>, which both read and write T, are generally invariant.

async-select-not-awaited.title: Assume Select(async ...) has completed the work
async-select-not-awaited.short: Continue without awaiting the Tasks produced by LINQ.
async-select-not-awaited.summary: Passing an async lambda to Select produces a sequence of Task values, not already-completed results.
async-select-not-awaited.why: You must enumerate the sequence to create the tasks and await those tasks to guarantee completion.
async-select-not-awaited.tips: Materialize the tasks and await Task.WhenAll for a clear pattern.

modify-list-during-foreach.title: Modify a List during foreach
modify-list-during-foreach.short: Change the collection while its enumerator is active.
modify-list-during-foreach.summary: Adding or removing items from List<T> during foreach invalidates the active enumerator.
modify-list-during-foreach.why: The enumerator expects the collection version to remain stable and fails when a structural change is detected.
modify-list-during-foreach.tips: For removal, consider RemoveAll; for complex transformations, build a separate result collection.

fire-and-forget-task.title: Lose failures with fire-and-forget Tasks
fire-and-forget-task.short: Start asynchronous work without awaiting or owning its lifetime.
fire-and-forget-task.summary: Discarding a Task means the caller does not wait for completion or failure, and the work can be cut short when its surrounding lifetime ends.
fire-and-forget-task.why: Exceptions from an unawaited Task do not flow back through the normal call path.
fire-and-forget-task.tips: For real background work, use an owned queue or hosted worker that manages lifetime and failures.

task-result-sync-blocking.title: Synchronously block on Task.Result
task-result-sync-blocking.short: Use .Result or .Wait() where the call chain can be asynchronous.
task-result-sync-blocking.summary: Synchronously waiting on async work occupies a thread and can deadlock under some SynchronizationContext implementations.
task-result-sync-blocking.why: await waits for completion without blocking the current thread and preserves the asynchronous call chain.
task-result-sync-blocking.tips: Prefer propagating async/await from the entry point through the call stack.

ignored-cancellation-token.title: Accept a CancellationToken but never use it
ignored-cancellation-token.short: Fail to propagate cancellation into lower-level work.
ignored-cancellation-token.summary: Receiving a token does not stop anything unless the method checks it or passes it to APIs that observe it.
ignored-cancellation-token.why: CancellationToken is cooperative, so the work itself must observe the request.
ignored-cancellation-token.tips: Pass the token to waits and I/O APIs whenever possible.

semaphore-release-finally.title: Forget to release SemaphoreSlim in finally
semaphore-release-finally.short: Leak a permit when protected work throws.
semaphore-release-finally.summary: If work after WaitAsync throws, a Release placed only on the success path never runs.
semaphore-release-finally.why: Leaked permits can eventually leave every future waiter blocked.
semaphore-release-finally.tips: After a successful acquisition, use try/finally to guarantee Release.

multiple-enumeration-side-effects.title: Enumerate IEnumerable more than once and repeat work
multiple-enumeration-side-effects.short: Reuse a deferred query that performs side effects or I/O each time.
multiple-enumeration-side-effects.summary: A deferred IEnumerable<T> may execute its source pipeline again on every enumeration.
multiple-enumeration-side-effects.why: For database, file, or logging-backed sequences, even Count followed by foreach can perform the work twice.
multiple-enumeration-side-effects.tips: Materialize with ToList or ToArray when the operation should run only once.

disposable-ownership.title: Dispose a borrowed resource
disposable-ownership.short: Dispose an IDisposable that is owned by the caller.
disposable-ownership.summary: Disposing a Stream or similar object received as an argument can make it unusable to the caller afterward.
disposable-ownership.why: API boundaries need a clear ownership contract describing who is responsible for Dispose.
disposable-ownership.tips: A simple rule is to dispose what you create and not dispose what you borrow unless the contract explicitly says otherwise.

datetime-unspecified-kind.title: Convert an Unspecified DateTime implicitly
datetime-unspecified-kind.short: Treat a clock value with no time-zone meaning as though its zone were known.
datetime-unspecified-kind.summary: A DateTime with Kind.Unspecified does not identify which time zone its clock value belongs to.
datetime-unspecified-kind.why: Conversion APIs must make an assumption, which can apply an offset different from the data's real meaning.
datetime-unspecified-kind.tips: Make the time zone explicit at system boundaries and consider DateTimeOffset.

culture-sensitive-string-comparison.title: Compare strings by calling ToLower()
culture-sensitive-string-comparison.short: Use culture-sensitive transformation and extra allocation just to compare values.
culture-sensitive-string-comparison.summary: Using ToLower for case-insensitive comparison can depend on the current culture and create extra strings.
culture-sensitive-string-comparison.why: StringComparison states the intended comparison semantics directly.
culture-sensitive-string-comparison.tips: Use Ordinal modes for identifiers and protocol values; choose an appropriate culture-aware comparison for natural language.

json-case-sensitive-properties.title: Assume JSON property-name casing will always match
json-case-sensitive-properties.short: Use serializer options that do not match the incoming JSON naming convention.
json-case-sensitive-properties.summary: Depending on System.Text.Json settings, differently-cased JSON names may not bind to C# properties.
json-case-sensitive-properties.why: The web defaults and general defaults differ in property-name behavior, so the chosen options matter.
json-case-sensitive-properties.tips: For fixed contracts, JsonPropertyNameAttribute can make the wire name explicit.

concurrent-dictionary-factory-repeat.title: Assume ConcurrentDictionary factories run only once
concurrent-dictionary-factory-repeat.short: Repeat expensive or side-effecting creation under contention.
concurrent-dictionary-factory-repeat.summary: GetOrAdd can invoke valueFactory concurrently more than once for the same key.
concurrent-dictionary-factory-repeat.why: Only one value is stored, but losing factory invocations can still execute.
concurrent-dictionary-factory-repeat.tips: If initialization must happen exactly once, consider storing Lazy<T> as the dictionary value.

whenall-failure-observation.title: Inspect only one failure from WhenAll
whenall-failure-observation.short: Miss additional failures when several tasks fault.
whenall-failure-observation.summary: When awaiting Task.WhenAll, the catch path observes a rethrown exception, but more than one child task may have failed.
whenall-failure-observation.why: The Task returned by WhenAll exposes the collected failures through its Exception property.
whenall-failure-observation.tips: Keep normal control flow simple, but inspect all failures for logging and diagnostics when needed.

http-request-failure.title: HttpRequestException: an HTTP request failed
http-request-failure.short: HttpClient could not complete request or response processing.
http-request-failure.summary: HttpRequestException represents failures around HTTP request execution, including connectivity problems and some status-handling paths.
http-request-failure.why: Possible causes include networking, DNS, TLS, and response status handling, so inspect the exception and available status information.
http-request-failure.tips: Do not retry every failure blindly; consider idempotency and whether the failure is transient.

json-deserialize-invalid.title: JsonException: JSON cannot be converted to the target type
json-deserialize-invalid.short: The JSON syntax or value shape does not match what the target type expects.
json-deserialize-invalid.summary: JsonException is thrown for malformed JSON and for values that cannot be converted into the requested .NET type.
json-deserialize-invalid.why: Path, location information, and inner exceptions can help identify the failing value.
json-deserialize-invalid.tips: Treat external input as untrusted and avoid logging complete sensitive payloads when reporting parse failures.

channel-closed-read.title: ChannelClosedException: read from a completed channel
channel-closed-read.short: Continue reading after a channel has completed and no values remain.
channel-closed-read.summary: ChannelClosedException can occur when reading from a completed channel that has no more data available.
channel-closed-read.why: Writer.Complete marks the end of the stream, so readers must include completion in their control flow.
channel-closed-read.tips: For continuous consumption, ReadAllAsync or WaitToReadAsync often makes completion easier to handle.

aggregate-task-failure.title: AggregateException: multiple failures were grouped
aggregate-task-failure.short: Several child failures were represented by one exception object.
aggregate-task-failure.summary: AggregateException carries multiple exceptions as a single exception.
aggregate-task-failure.why: Parallel APIs and synchronous Task waiting can collect child failures in InnerExceptions.
aggregate-task-failure.tips: In asynchronous code, prefer await and inspect the aggregate task only when diagnostics need all failures.

cs0120-instance-member.title: CS0120: an object reference is required
cs0120-instance-member.short: Access an instance member directly from a static context.
cs0120-instance-member.summary: CS0120 occurs when code references an instance member without identifying the object instance.
cs0120-instance-member.why: A static method has no this reference, so the compiler cannot know which object's member should be used.
cs0120-instance-member.tips: Make the method an instance method or access the member through an explicit object.

cs0165-unassigned-local.title: CS0165: use of unassigned local variable
cs0165-unassigned-local.short: Read a local variable that is not definitely assigned on every path.
cs0165-unassigned-local.summary: CS0165 is produced when definite-assignment analysis cannot prove a local has a value before it is read.
cs0165-unassigned-local.why: If assignment happens only in one branch, another control-flow path can reach the read without a value.
cs0165-unassigned-local.tips: Initialize at declaration or ensure every path assigns the variable first.

cs0266-explicit-conversion.title: CS0266: cannot implicitly convert type
cs0266-explicit-conversion.short: Attempt a potentially lossy conversion without making it explicit.
cs0266-explicit-conversion.summary: CS0266 occurs when no implicit conversion exists between the source and destination types.
cs0266-explicit-conversion.why: A conversion such as double to int can lose fractional or range information, so the intent must be explicit.
cs0266-explicit-conversion.tips: Before casting, decide how rounding, range limits, and checked overflow behavior should work.

cs1503-argument-type.title: CS1503: argument cannot convert to parameter type
cs1503-argument-type.short: Pass a value whose type does not match the method parameter.
cs1503-argument-type.summary: CS1503 occurs when an argument cannot be converted to the corresponding parameter type.
cs1503-argument-type.why: Overload resolution checks whether arguments can convert to candidate parameter types, and reports failure when none fit.
cs1503-argument-type.tips: Check the API signature and provide the correct type or choose an appropriate overload.

cs8602-possible-null.title: CS8602: dereference of a possibly null reference
cs8602-possible-null.short: Dereference a nullable value without proving it is non-null.
cs8602-possible-null.summary: CS8602 is reported when nullable flow analysis considers an expression possibly null at a member access.
cs8602-possible-null.why: At runtime the same path could throw NullReferenceException, so the warning points to missing flow information or validation.
cs8602-possible-null.tips: Use a null check, pattern matching, or a clearer API contract to prove the value is non-null.

cs8618-nonnullable-init.title: CS8618: non-nullable member is not initialized
cs8618-nonnullable-init.short: The compiler cannot prove a non-nullable member has a value after construction.
cs8618-nonnullable-init.summary: CS8618 is reported when a non-nullable field or property is not definitely initialized by the end of object construction.
cs8618-nonnullable-init.why: The type says the member will not be null, but the construction paths do not satisfy that contract.
cs8618-nonnullable-init.tips: Initialize it in a constructor, use required, or make the member nullable if null is genuinely valid.
